Kodak continues the theme of a serious relationship by showing interest in the girl’s heritage. St. Lucia is a volcanic island nation in the Eastern Caribbean known for its French-Creole culture.

line: It’s something about that girl, know I’m so attracted to her I’m so fuckin’ mad ’cause she almost got away I just wan’ kidnap her, trap her, bag her No more bein’ casual, fly dates on private planes, ayy
vault_lines: I just wanna flex her, flex her, flex her
meaning:
In these lines, Kodak uses high-stakes, figurative language to describe his desire for a committed relationship.


The Motivation: Kodak admits his frustration (“so fuckin' mad”) that his previous “Push-Pull” game almost caused the girl to leave for good. This realization acts as the catalyst for him dropping his “casual” persona.
The Metaphors: Terms like “kidnap,” “trap,” and “bag” are used figuratively here to mean “locking her down” or making her his exclusive partner. In this context, “trapping” her isn’t about restriction, but about securing the relationship so she doesn’t “get away” again.
The Lifestyle Shift: He contrasts “casual” dating with “fly dates on private planes.” This signifies a move from low-effort “situationships” to a high-level, serious partnership where he is willing to invest both his emotions and his wealth.



By using such strong terminology, Kodak emphasizes that his attraction is no longer a “game"—it has become an obsession with ensuring she stays in his life permanently.

line: I just wish that Jessica could just forgive me Give me one more chance, all I ask for, Jess
vault_lines: I just wish that Jessica could just forgive me
meaning:
In these lines, Kodak addresses a specific woman named Jessica, pleading for her forgiveness. However, the line concludes with a clever phonetic play on words.

When spoken aloud, “Jess” sounds nearly identical to “Yes.” By placing it immediately after the phrase “all I ask for,” Kodak creates a double meaning:


The Direct Appeal: He is calling out to “Jess” specifically, making the plea personal and urgent.
The Desired Answer: He is literally stating that a “Yes” is “all he asks for” in response to his request for a second chance.



This technique allows Kodak to show vulnerability while maintaining the wordplay-heavy style he is known for, turning a simple name into the very answer he’s hoping to hear.

Kodak Black was placed into a youth detention center three times in one year, and then placed on probation.

In October 2015, he was arrested in Pompano Beach and charged with robbery, battery, false imprisonment of a child, and possession of cannabis. He was later released.

In April 2016, Kodak Black was arrested in Hallandale Beach, Florida and charged with possession of a weapon by a convicted felon, possession of marijuana, and fleeing from officers.

The following month of May 2016, he was arrested in Broward County, Florida and charged with armed robbery and false imprisonment. He was detained in custody.

In August 2016, he appeared in court in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Several executives from Atlantic Records attended the court; vice-president Michael Kushner commented “Black has a bright future as a recording artist”. Kodak Black pleaded no contest to all charges and under a plea agreement was to be placed on house arrest for one year, have five years probation, perform community service as required, and take anger management classes. He would also be permitted to tour internationally. Prior to his release from Broward Main Jail, police discovered two outstanding criminal warrants, the first from Florence, South Carolina alleging felony criminal sexual conduct, the second from St. Lucie County, Florida alleging two counts of misdemeanor marijuana possession. Kodak Black was not released from jail.

In September 2016, Kodak Black pleaded no contest to two misdemeanor drug charges and was sentenced to four months in jail. He was credited for time spent in custody awaiting trial and was required to serve 120 days. He was also suspended from driving for one year.

Kodak Black was released from jail in Florida, and was then transported to Florence, South Carolina to face charges of sexual assault. According to the female victim, who reported the incident to her school nurse, she had attended a February 2016 performance by Kodak Black at “Treasure City” in Florence, after which she accompanied him to his hotel room where he is alleged to have told her he “couldn’t help himself” as he tore off her clothes, bit her repeatedly, and raped her as she screamed for help. Kodak Black was released from custody in South Carolina on December 1, 2016 after posting a $100,000 bond, but returned to court on February 8, 2017. About Kodak Black, the Miami New Times asked “is he the product of larger societal problems, having been raised on a steady diet of misogynistic rap lyrics?” Within hours of release, he recorded and released “There He Go”, a single which mentions his recent release from jail:

Just hopped off the plane I just got out about a day ago
Everybody love me, when they see me they be like, “There he go!”
Got me a new lady, we ‘bout to take a trip to Mexico
Crackers took my .40 so I’m 'bout to go buy a Draco (an AK-47 rifle)

In February 2017, Kodak Black was arrested again for violation of his probation. He was held without bond and his musical tour was postponed.

In April 2017, Kodak Black was indicted by a grand jury in South Carolina, and was scheduled to go on trial in April 2019 in Florence, South Carolina on a charge of first-degree criminal sexual conduct. This was later postponed. Also in April 2017, he appeared in court in Florida, where his anger management counselor Ramona Sanchez spoke about him disrupting her class. Sanchez said he was constantly burping during her class, and when asked to leave, he refused. When Sanchez threatened to call 911, he grabbed her phone and her wrist. The counselor recommended that Kodak Black participate in individual therapy instead of group therapy.

On May 4, 2017, he was sentenced for violating his house arrest to 364 days in the Broward County Jail, with the possibility of an early release if he completes a life skills course. He was released on June 5, 2017. He will remain on house arrest for one year, and five years of probation.

line: Girl, I’m done with you (With you) Girl, we done, it’s through (Girl, we done)

meaning:
Borrowing Gucci Mane’s famous ad-lib, Kodak Black gives it a metaphorical meaning here. By starting the song and its hook with the end of a relationship, the gimmicky “SKRT” sounds like a quick turn in life, a restart.

A heartbreak or an ending love story have long been considered a rite of passage, especially from the teenage years to adulthood. It is also a common theme for Black. On this song, the idea of a car starting really fast or taking a quick turn —making it burn its tires in a “SKRT” sound— mimics this theme. The rest of the song follows a similar logic by referring to the end of school or the rapper’s new financial success as opposed to its rather poor past.

By repeating “SKRT”, Black metaphorically depicts this song as a fresh start. Coincidentally, this was also one of Black’s breakthrough singles.

line: I can’t even go to sleep (Why?) I’m rolling on a bean (Yeah)
vault_lines: I can't even go to sleep (Why?)
meaning:
“Bean” is one of many street names for the drug molly, or MDMA, which is known to stimulate feelings of energy and ecstasy from the user. Usually, after a high on a stimulant, the user struggles to sleep that night.



Kodak particularly changes the usual idiom, “off the bean” to “rolling on a bean” to accomplish two things. Firstly, he wants to relate back to the theme and title (Roll In Peace) of the song–due to fame and legal trouble, Kodak has a hard time enjoying life because of public fascination and intense media scrutiny. Thus, Kodak uses drugs like molly to find some peace of mind and escape the pressures of daily life created by the media.

On the other hand, Kodak could be using the word “roll” to depict the cyclical nature of using dopamine targeting drugs such as MDMA. Because it is similar to a stimulant, molly spikes dopamine levels in the brain for a short period causing the user to feel overly happy, after which levels crash which leads to depression. In order to feel happy again, the user is forced to get high, thus creating a vicious cycle of happiness and depression.

It’s also worth noting, in conjunction with the line immediately prior, this could also be a reference to “The Princess and the Pea”, a fairy tale in which a small bean disturbs a princess from falling asleep.

Some rare forms, sometimes common amongst speakers of Japanese, Albanian, and many other languages, include subject-object-verb, verb-subject-object, or even object-subject-verb. Although X doesn’t use one of these forms, it sounds as though he is to amplify the allusion to Yoda.

line: I swapped out the mic for the gun I swapped out the ice for the mud I swapped out the spice for the bud
vault_lines: I swapped out the mic for the gun
meaning:
In these three lines Kodak is referencing changes he’s made in the items and substances he uses in the course of his lifestyle.

In keeping with the thugged out theme of the song, the first line states he is swapping his microphone for a gun indicating that he is primarily a thug and not a rapper.

The second and third lines relate to his choice of narcotics.  “Ice” is slang for crystal meth, a cheap and potent methamphetamine, whereas ‘mud’ is a slang term for promethazine-codeine cough syrup, which is far more expensive due to its scarcity and popularity.  Similarly, “spice” is a cheap, synthetic version of weed vs. “bud”, which refers to the flowers of a natural marijuana plant.

Kodak is implying he is going back to his thug lifestyle but has significantly upgraded the price and quality of his drugs at the same time.

Riff on the proverb “live by the sword, die by the sword,” which comes from Matthew 26:52:

Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.

The implication in both the proverb and the biblical passage is that those who advocate violence will die by violence, and that we should instead focus on nonviolence as a path forward.

In this instance, “play” refers to the game of the streets, one often marked by violence, and “lay” stands in as an euphemism for death, specifically being placed in a coffin. While Kodak riffs well upon the proverb, he seems to be either missing or ignoring the usual call to peaceful actions implied with phrase, and instead uses it as a means to assert his own power.

1800 block refers to the 1800 Block of Golden Acres, the public housing project in Pompano Beach, Florida where Kodak grew up. It’s his most iconic territorial reference almost a brand that he drops throughout his catalog to signal he never forgot where he came from, even after fame and prison time.

[Bake] is a shoutout to a close associate from the neighborhood. The brackets in most transcriptions suggest even fans couldn’t make out the name clearly, which actually reinforces the point: Kodak isn’t namedropping for clout, he’s speaking directly to his people.

The line lands right after he mentions being locked up with “everything on wait” so repping the block and shouting out a homie is his way of saying I stayed solid no matter what.

line: Choppin’ heads and burnin’ houses, nigga
vault_lines: Choppin' heads and burnin' houses, nigga
meaning:
The next line Kodak says after this is “Koupe tèt, boule kay” which is the exact same thing translated in Haitian creole.

“Koupe tèt, boule kay!” was the war cry of Jean Jacques-Dessalines, the general who lead the formally-enslaved people of Haiti to victory against the French in 1804.



This motto greatly defines his persona and the type of general he was. Dessalines took over the fight for Haitian independence after Toussaint Louverture was captured by the French in 1802.

Compared to Louverture, Dessalines had little to no mercy (being enslaved can do that to you) and was not going to compromise with the French under any circumstances (as Toussaint Louverture often tried to). His motto was “chop their heads, burn their houses!” Koupe tèt, boule kay.

As you could imagine, Dessalines taking over was the beginning of the bloodiest point in the Haitian war of independence, but he would ultimately lead them to victory in 1804, declaring Haiti the 2nd independent nation in the Americas, the first american nation ruled by black people, and most importantly, the first nation to permanently abolish slavery. He renamed the country from the french “Saint-Domingue” to “Ayiti,” which was the original name the native Tainos gave to the island.

It should also be noted that after Dessalines declared victory and declared Haiti independent, he went on to massacre all the remaining French people on the island. From this, it is easy to see how ruthless he was as a general and why he would be saying shit like “Koupe tèt, boule kay!”

Kodak creates a thematic bridge between his lifestyle and the discography of Drake. By mentioning “Marvin room,” he is referencing Drake’s 2011 hit “Marvins Room” from the album Take Care.


The Location: Historically, “Marvin’s Room” refers to the legendary recording studio in Hollywood formerly owned by Marvin Gaye, where Drake recorded much of his early work.
The Mood: In hip-hop culture, “Marvins Room” has become synonymous with “late-night,” “vulnerable,” or “temporary” energy. By choosing this location over his own home (“my place”), Kodak suggests a desire for distance or a situation that is strictly about the “vibe” rather than a personal, domestic connection.



The follow-up line—where he mentions a personal conversation with Drake—acts as a “meta” confirmation of the reference, showing that Kodak isn’t just a fan of the music but is now a peer who has earned Drake’s “admiration.”

Kodak uses a “sensory” juxtaposition to highlight the difference between his environment and his personal status.



Gunpowder: Represents the violence and danger of the streets. If it “smells like gunpowder,” it implies a recent shootout or a high-tension situation in the neighborhood.







Jimmy Choo: A luxury fashion house famous for its high-end fragrances.





Kodak is flexing his “elevation.” He is claiming that even when he is in dangerous situations where “gunpowder” is in the air, he still carries the scent and aura of a wealthy superstar. It’s a metaphor for remaining “untouchable"—he is present in the struggle, but he smells like success.

line: Steppin’ on niggas, now my toe hurt

meaning:
Kodak uses a humorous double entendre to illustrate his dominance over his rivals.

In street slang, “stepping” on someone refers to exerting power or crushing the competition. By claiming his “toe hurts,” Kodak suggests that he has defeated so many enemies and been “at their necks” for so long that he is experiencing physical fatigue from the sheer amount of winning he’s doing.

It’s a “flex” that portrays his dominance as constant and effortless, yet so frequent that it’s become a “chore” to stay at the top. This also aligns with the track’s theme of success bringing both satisfaction and exhaustion.

line: ’Cause I was 1800 block like I’m Peyton Manning

meaning:
Peyton Manning is a legendary, Hall of Fame NFL quarterback who famously wore the number 18 throughout his entire professional career with the Indianapolis Colts and the Denver Broncos.

Kodak uses this as a “numerical” play to reference his home:


The 1800 Block: This refers to the Golden Acres housing projects in Pompano Beach, Florida, where Kodak grew up. The neighborhood is often referred to as the “1800 block.”
The Connection: By linking the “1800 block” to “18” Peyton Manning, Kodak is claiming that he is the “MVP” or the star of his neighborhood.

line: They don’t wanna see you ridin’ in a panoramic

meaning:
Here, Kodak uses the “panoramic” roof—a large glass ceiling found in high-end luxury SUVs like the Rolls-Royce Cullinan or Lamborghini Urus—as a symbol of his elevated status.



A panoramic roof literally makes the driver more visible to the outside world. By saying people “don’t want to see” him in one, Kodak is touching on the theme of envy. In his community, “ridin' in a panoramic” means you’ve “made it” out of the struggle and into a level of wealth where you can afford a half-million-dollar vehicle.

The line reflects the song’s title, “All Love,” ironically. While he shows love, he acknowledges that his success makes others uncomfortable. They would prefer to see him back in the “trenches” rather than enjoying the literal and metaphorical “clear view” that success (and a panoramic roof) provides.
